name: Net debt
seoTitle: Net debt Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Net debt: work out long-term debt (Net debt) from the cash and the accounts payable. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Net debt calculator works out long-term debt (Net debt) from the cash, the accounts payable, the current portion of the long term debt and the other payables or accrued items. It is built for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Net debt calculator work?
sections.html:
The Net debt calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports long-term debt (Net debt) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the cash, the accounts payable, the current portion of the long term debt and the other payables or accrued items (Short-term debt).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Net debt calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Long-term debt=cash and cash equivalents + net debt − short-term debt
Cash equivalents=-cash + cash and cash equivalents
Current part of leases=-accounts payable − current portion of the long term debt − other payables or accrued items + short-term debt
Non-current part of leases=long-term debt − non-current long term debt − other payables or accrued items
Long-term debt=long-term debt
Short-term debt=short-term debt

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Cash and cash equivalents = 10, Short-term debt = 10 and Net debt = 10. The calculator returns Cash and cash equivalents = 10, Short-term debt = 10 and Long-term debt = 10.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Cash and cash equivalents = 10, Short-term debt = 10 and Long-term debt = 10 should be roughly the size you expected from Cash and cash equivalents = 10 and Short-term debt = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Net debt calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the cash, the accounts payable and the current portion of the long term debt — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Net debt calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns long-term debt (Net debt), derived from the cash, the accounts payable and the current portion of the long term debt. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Net debt calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the cash, the accounts payable, the current portion of the long term debt and the other payables or accrued items, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter cash in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Cash opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Cash and cash equivalents = 10. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Net debt calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
